articles.title: Social Security spousal benefits: How they work for married and divorced spouses
articles.summary: You may qualify for Social Security spousal benefits at age 62 if you're married or divorced if the marriage lasted 10 years. Learn how spousal benefits work...
articles.body:

Social Security spousal benefits provide a monthly payment based on a partner's earnings history that's worth up to 50% of the partner's benefit at full retirement age. If you're at least 62 and married or divorced, you may qualify for spousal benefits even if you never worked. Here's how it works.

Social Security spousal benefits are retirement payments that are based on your spouse's earnings record instead of your own work history. The maximum spousal benefit is 50% of your spouse's primary insurance amount (PIA), or the benefit they qualify for at full retirement age (FRA), which is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.

It's possible to collect spousal Social Security even if you're divorced. But as you'll see shortly, the rules are a bit different for current spouses versus ex-spouses.

Spousal benefits can be an essential part of retirement planning if you didn't work much outside the home or your partner significantly outearned you. But if you're eligible for a spousal benefit and your own retirement benefit, you'll receive the larger of the two, but not both. (Technically, Social Security gives you your retirement benefit first, then tops off the payment with any additional funds you're entitled to through spousal benefits.)

If you worked enough to qualify for Social Security, your own retirement benefit may be more than your spousal benefit, even if you didn't earn much. According to Social Security Administration data, 2.9% of recipients get spousal benefits.

Who qualifies for spousal benefit eligibility?

To claim spousal Social Security, you typically need to be at least 62. However, you can collect spousal benefits at any age if your partner receives a retirement or disability benefit and you care for their qualifying child (one who's younger than 16 or has a disability). Eligibility requirements differ for current and former spouses.

If you're currently married, you may qualify for spousal benefits if:

Your spouse is already claiming Social Security.

You've been married for at least a year (exceptions apply).

The marriage lasted at least 10 consecutive years.

You've been divorced for at least two years, and your ex is 62 or older, OR your ex is already collecting Social Security.

The average monthly Social Security spousal benefit was around $987 as of September 2026, according to Social Security Administration data. This number is significantly less than the little over $2,088 the average retired worker receives.

Social Security payments for spouses are capped at half of the working spouse's FRA benefit. Claiming spousal benefits before you reach full retirement age reduces this amount even further. If you claim as soon as you're eligible at 62, you'd only receive 32.5% of your spouse's PIA.

If you're eligible for your own retirement benefit, you can choose to delay past your full retirement age and earn an extra 8% per year until you're 70, courtesy of delayed retirement credits. But spousal benefits don't let you earn delayed retirement credits. You'll collect your maximum spousal benefit at FRA, which is 67 for most people.

Suppose your spouse's primary insurance amount is $3,000. You never worked outside the home, but since you've been married for 30 years, you're entitled to a spousal benefit.

Your maximum spousal benefit is $1,500, or 50% of your partner's $3,000 PIA.

Your spouse can wait until 70 to collect, which would increase their monthly check to $3,720.

But the most you'd receive is $1,500, plus any future cost-of-living adjustments. You can't earn delayed retirement credits by waiting past your own full retirement age.

But Social Security would reduce your spousal payment if you claimed early (unless you care for your spouse's qualifying child). Starting immediately after you turn 62 would lower your benefit to 32.5% of your spouse's PIA. Instead of your maximum $1,500 benefit, you'd only receive $975.

You need at least 40 work credits, or 10 years of full-time work, to qualify for a Social Security retirement benefit. But if you've never worked outside of the home, you have a limited work record, you only worked part time, or your spouse significantly outearned you, spousal benefits let you collect Social Security.

Social Security doesn't have a separate benefit category for non-working spouses. When you apply, Social Security determines whether you qualify for a retirement benefit based on your own earnings and a spousal benefit based on your partner's earnings. You may be eligible for Social Security as a non-working spouse, even if you don't qualify for your own retirement benefit, if you meet the requirements for spousal benefits.

How claiming a spousal benefit affects other benefits

Claiming a spousal benefit won't affect your partner or ex-partner's benefit. If you're divorced and your ex has remarried, your spousal benefits also won't impact payments to your ex or anyone else who collects their Social Security, like their current spouse if they've remarried.

That's because Social Security simply uses the earnings history of the working partner to qualify the person's spouse or ex-spouse for benefits; the payments aren't subtracted from the benefits the working partner earned.

Spousal benefits also don't affect survivor benefits, which are a different category of Social Security that we'll cover in the next section.

If you worked enough to claim Social Security on your own, spousal benefits can only increase your retirement benefit. Social Security will calculate your retirement payment, then add any extra funds you're entitled to from spousal benefits.

Spousal benefits versus survivor benefits

Spousal benefits are based on the earnings record of a living current or former spouse, while survivor benefits are based on the work history of someone who has died. The following family members may be eligible for survivor benefits:

Children 17 and younger (or 18 or 19, if they're enrolled full time in K-12 school) or who have a disability that began before age 22

Parents 62 or older if the person who died provided most of their support

There are some key differences between spousal benefits and survivor benefits for spouses:

Claiming age: Social Security claiming age is 62 for most people, but you can file for survivor benefits when you turn 60 (or 50 if you're disabled).

Benefit amount: You can receive up to 100% of the benefit your late spouse was entitled to through survivor benefits, but the maximum spousal benefit is 50% of the working spouse's primary insurance amount. Claiming early can reduce your payments to as little as 71.5%. If you start spousal benefits as soon as you turn 62 and your full retirement age is 67, you'll receive just 32.5% of your spouse's PIA.

Remarriage rules: You can't collect divorced spouse benefits if you're currently married. However, you can still receive survivor benefits if you remarry after you turn 60 (or 50 if you're disabled).

Rules for switching benefits: You can no longer claim a spousal benefit and then switch to your own retirement benefit. However, you can claim survivor benefits and apply for retirement benefits later, which can allow you to earn delayed retirement credits.

How do spousal benefits and survivor benefits compare?

Current spouses married at least one year (some exceptions appply)

Spouses married at least nine months (some exceptions apply).

Ex-spouse: no, if divorced at least two years

Surviving spouses keep benefits if remaried at 60 or later (50 if disabled); remarrying before 60 generally pauses them, but they may be resumed if the new marriage ends

Outdated claiming strategies to be aware of

In the past, many couples used two strategies to maximize Social Security benefits, both of which were eliminated by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015:

Filing a restricted application: If you qualified for both spousal and retirement benefits, you could file a restricted application for spousal benefits only once you reached full retirement age, then switch to a larger retirement benefit later, typically at age 70, after taking advantage of 8% delayed retirement credits for each year you waited.

The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 largely nixed this strategy by expanding Social Security's "deemed filing" rules. Essentially, if you were born on Jan. 2, 1954, or later and you qualify for spousal and retirement benefits, Social Security "deems" you to be filing for both benefits and gives you the larger of the two. You can't claim a spousal benefit and switch to your higher retirement benefit later.

File and suspend: To qualify for Social Security using your current spouse's work record, they need to be receiving benefits. Before the 2015 law, the working spouse could apply for benefits at FRA to allow their spouse to receive spousal payments, then immediately suspend their own benefits. They'd resume benefits again after earning delayed retirement credits, usually at age 70. Now, if someone files for Social Security and suspends their benefit, any spousal benefits or payments to other family members are generally suspended too.

How and when to apply for spousal benefits

Applying for spousal benefits is the same as applying for regular Social Security. You can apply up to four months before you want to start claiming benefits. But remember, your spousal benefit will be reduced if you claim before your FRA.

You can apply for spousal benefits online, by phone, or by visiting an office. You may need a few additional documents or information, like your marriage certificate, divorce decree, or your current or former spouse's date of birth and Social Security number.

But you don't need to delay your application if you don't have all the required info: Social Security says it will help you locate the information and documents you need.

Common mistakes to avoid when claiming spousal benefits

Avoid these common mistakes if you expect to claim spousal benefits:

Overestimating your benefit: Spousal benefits are usually modest since they're limited to half of the working spouse's PIA, so make sure you have an accurate picture of how much you can expect. Create a My Social Security account to get an estimate of any spousal or retirement benefits you may be eligible for.

Claiming too early: If you start spousal Social Security at 62, you'll receive just 32.5% of your partner's PIA. Consider waiting until your full retirement age to claim if you expect spousal payments to be an important source of retirement income.

Delaying your claim: Be sure to file your claim by your FRA. Waiting longer won't boost your spousal payments, so you'll be leaving money on the table.

Not applying because you don't have some documents: You may need to provide documents like a marriage or divorce record to claim spousal benefits, but don't hold off on filing if you can't find a document. Social Security can often help you find whatever you need to complete your application.

Can I collect spousal benefits and my own retirement benefit at the same time?

No. If you're eligible for both spousal and retirement benefits, Social Security will give you the larger of the two.

The maximum Social Security spousal benefit is 50% of your spouse's primary insurance amount. To collect the maximum benefit, you'll typically need to wait until your full retirement age (67 for most people). If you claim at 62, you'll receive just 32.5% of your spouse's full benefit.

Yes, you may be able to collect Social Security on your ex-spouse's record if you were married for 10 years or more. If your ex hasn't started taking benefits yet, you'll need to have been divorced for at least two years.

At what age can I start collecting spousal benefits?

You can usually start collecting spousal benefits at age 62, but your benefit will be reduced to 32.5% of your spouse's PIA. You'll qualify for your full spousal benefit at FRA, which is 67 if you were born after 1959. You can claim at any age if your spouse receives retirement or disability benefits, and you care for their qualifying child.

What happens to my spousal benefit if my spouse dies?

You can switch from spousal benefits to survivor benefits if your spouse dies. Survivor benefits are higher than spousal benefits, providing up to 100% of your late spouse's benefit.

Can I switch from a spousal benefit to my own retirement benefit later?

No, the 2015 Bipartisan Budget Act nixed this once-common claiming strategy for couples. Now, if you're eligible for both retirement and spousal benefits when you apply, Social Security requires or "deems" you to file for both benefits and gives you the larger of the two.

What documents do I need to apply for spousal benefits?

To apply for spousal benefits, you may need to provide your birth certificate (or proof of citizenship) and Social Security number, your spouse's birth date and Social Security number, as well as your marriage or divorce certificate.

Mortgage rates continue to rise as 2026 nears its end. What is the outlook for home loan rates in the next five years? An AI-generated forecast looks for mortgage rates to remain above 6% through 2031; however, bear and bull scenarios are wide-ranging. Mortgage interest rates are determined by several factors , all of which can give us clues about the future.

Mortgage rates are tuned to the government bond market

One of the most useful indicators for predicting mortgage rates is the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note . Mortgage rates and 10-year Treasury yields typically move in the same direction, although mortgage rates are usually higher because lenders factor in additional risks. This difference is known as the spread, and we'll account for it when estimating where mortgage rates could go.

With that in mind, the first step is to look at where economists believe Treasury yields are headed over the next five years. To build a forecast, we'll combine expert economic projections with data compiled using artificial intelligence.

Economists' 5-year forecast for Treasury rates

Michael Wolf, a global economist at Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Ltd., outlined the firm's Treasury yield expectations over the next five years in a September update from the Deloitte Global Economics Research Center .

"After delivering three quarter-point interest rate cuts in the second half of last year, the Federal Reserve reversed course and raised interest rates at its September meeting. We now expect the Fed to hike once more before the end of this year. As consumer spending growth and inflation moderate in 2027, we expect the Fed will begin to cut rates again at the end of that year. We have significantly raised our expectations for the 10-year Treasury yield," he wrote.

Here's the Deloitte 10-year Treasury five-year forecast.

Meanwhile, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that the 10-year Treasury yield will reach 4.4% by 2031, and remain there through 2036.

Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence compiled the predictions into a consensus forecast, which we will utilize below.

As mentioned, the 10-year Treasury and 30-year fixed mortgage rates are separated by a spread. That difference between the two has been on either side of 2.5 percentage points in recent years. That's a significant change when compared to the spread from 2010 to 2020, when it was under two percentage points (and often near 1.5).

Using a 2.0 percentage point spread, here's an example of how Treasurys and mortgage rates compare:

Here's a recent example: As of October 15, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.40% and 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.098%. The spread was 7.40- - 5.09 = 2.31 percentage points.

Claude AI noted the recent significant widening in the spread in its revised analysis. The base case for Claude's spread assumptions now begins at 2.15 percentage points in 2027, gradually declining to 1.98 percentage points in 2031.

"The 10-yr Treasury surged from 4.74% to ~5.25% (+51 bps) and the 30-yr mortgage from 6.71% to 7.40% (+69 bps) in six weeks. The Fed hiked in September 2026. All scenarios [have been] revised materially upward," Claude wrote.

Using these spread estimates, we can now complete our five-year mortgage rate forecast.

Using the Treasury forecast, we add the Claude-suggested base case assumed spread between the bond market and 30-year fixed mortgage rates to compile a five-year forecast:

For its base case, Claude slightly modified the Treasury forecast from above, adding its forecasted spread between the bond market and 30-year fixed mortgage rates to compile a five-year forecast:

While this forecast is for a base case with gradual normalization to the spread, the easing of inflation, and the Fed cutting rates slowly beginning in late 2027, Claude AI also prepared a "bull" estimate and a "bear" estimate:

The bull case: "The Fed pivots early 2027, inflation returns to 2%, AI debt cycle moderates." In that case, Claude predicts 30-year home loan rates to move from 6.55% in 2027 to 5.38% in 2031.

The bear case: "Yields breach 6%, fiscal spiral, AI debt binge keeps term premium elevated." In this scenario, Claude sees the 30-year mortgage rate move from 7.7% in 2027, up to 8.05% in 2028, and then gradually falling to 7.25% by 2031

Of course, these are long-range estimates based on historical norms and broad expectations. All of these numbers could be thrown out the window if any of the following happens:

The 10-year Treasurys outperform or underperform the forecast. For example, yields could crash in a severe economic setback, such as a recession , or soar on mounting government deficits. We've seen just how unpredictable interest rates can be with wild cards such as geopolitical unrest.

The spread between Treasurys and mortgage rates narrows — or dramatically widens.

Monetary policy, as driven by the Federal Reserve , substantially changes.

Mortgage rate predictions for the next 5 years: FAQs

Will mortgage interest rates ever be 3% again?

There is no forecast that predicts a 3% mortgage rate in the next five years. However, who saw such low home loan rates on the horizon in 2007 when rates were about where they are now? Things like the Great Recession and a global pandemic are rarely on the radar, and such drastic events are what it takes to move mortgage rates into the cellar.

The analysis above predicts 2027 mortgage rates to be near 6.95%.

Will mortgage rates drop in the next 5 years?

Based on the estimates above, mortgage rates are expected to moderate in the next five years, but remain above 6%. However, a recession or other unknown disruption to the economy (such as war, a financial collapse or another pandemic) could steepen the drop in rates.

Is it better to fix a rate for 2 or 5 years?

If you are considering an adjustable-rate mortgage with an initial fixed-rate period, you will first want to consider how long you will actually remain in the house you are financing. Then the long-term mortgage rate forecasting begins. The best approach is probably to select the initial term that best suits your current budget.

articles.title: We have a $300,000 mortgage with a 2.75% interest rate. I want to pay it off. My husband says I’m crazy. Who’s right?
articles.summary: “I don’t want to enter retirement owing six figures when we have the cash to clear it.”
articles.body:
I'm 57 and my husband is 59. We've been married 26 years, and our two kids, 24 and 27, support themselves. We bought our house in 2003 for $410,000, and it's now worth about $720,000. We owe $300,000 at 2.75%, with a payment of $2,150 a month.

We both work. I make $135,000 a year and he makes $165,000. We have about $1.5 million in 401(k)s and IRAs, plus $400,000 in savings, Treasury bills and short-term investments. He has a small pension, we'll both get Social Security, and we have no other debt.

We've never carried a credit-card balance, and we pay cash for our cars. Neither of us grew up with money. I remember my parents arguing about it at the kitchen table. I want to use $300,000 of our cash to pay off the mortgage. My husband says that's irrational.

At 2.75% interest, he says, we can earn more by investing, and paying it off would lock up money we might need. He's partly right about the numbers. But I want one part of our finances that can't be lost, and I don't want to enter retirement owing six figures when we have the cash to pay it off.

We have about $420,000 in equity. He's a much more aggressive investor than I am. During the pandemic he got into tech stocks and crypto, and we lost about $25,000 on a position that peaked around $90,000. He calls that minor compared with his gains, but I don't.

Last year, he bought a stock because someone at his gym called it the next Nvidia. I prefer index funds. I've started checking our accounts after he trades, and I resent being put in that role. The bigger problem is that he makes decisions without telling me.

Three months ago, he moved $60,000 from our joint savings into a brokerage account because he thought the market would run away from us. I only found out while checking our balance. He said he assumed I'd be fine with it since the money was still ours.

He says I'm trying to control him, but I don't want to control his money. I want him to stop treating our joint money as his own. My compromise suggestion was to pay off the mortgage with $300,000, keep $100,000 as an emergency fund, and continue contributing to our retirement.

articles.title: Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at Age 70
articles.summary: Waiting until 70 maximizes your monthly check, but the break-even math may surprise you.
articles.body:
As of December 2025, the average Social Security benefit for people aged 70 is $2,274.68 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). This age marks the absolute ceiling for your monthly check's growth. Credits stop accruing once your 70th birthday arrives, so there isn't any financial reason to wait longer to claim.

Waiting past your full retirement age (FRA) -- 67 for most workers today -- triggers delayed retirement credits . The SSA adds an 8% increase for every full year you delay past that point. If your FRA is 67, this mechanic can add up to 24% to your base amount if you hold off until age 70.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The average check for 70-year-olds reflects a wide range of work histories and earlier claiming decisions. While many in this group didn't wait until 70 to claim, those who maxed out delayed retirement credits see significantly higher starting amounts. Many retirees claim earlier to cover immediate costs, which keeps the population average lower than the theoretical maximum.

The gender gap remains visible in this age group. Men receive an average benefit of $2,529.62 per month, while women receive $2,024.08 per month, a gap of about $505.54. This difference often stems from historical wage disparities and differences in years spent in the workforce.

Benefit amounts are as of December 2025, the most recent data available from the SSA.

Delaying until 70 is often a calculated move for those in good health. It fits people with a history of family longevity or those with a lower-earning spouse. Because the survivor benefit -- the benefit your partner qualifies for after you die -- steps up when the higher-earning spouse waits, this choice can protect a household's income for decades.

You'll generally need to live until age 82 or 83 to reach the break-even point. This is where the larger checks finally catch up to the total amount you'd have received if you'd claimed earlier. If you live an average lifespan, you tend to receive roughly the same total regardless of when you claim.

The SSA bases your benefit on an average of your wages across your 35 highest-earning years. It adjusts earlier wages for inflation and runs them through the primary insurance amount formula.

articles.title: Kevin O’Leary says his golden money rule could make you a millionaire — even on a $68K salary. Are you missing out?
articles.summary: Mr. Wonderful’s advice could be your diamond-encrusted ticket to financial freedom.
articles.body:

For a man who loves flashy suits and diamond-encrusted jewelry, Kevin O'Leary keeps his investing advice pretty simple. Barebones even.

"What piece of advice do I give my kids over and over and over again about money? Don't spend it, save it, invest it, let it compound — that's the gift the market gives you," O'Leary said in a video posted to his Instagram (1).

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

"Take 15% of all your paychecks, all your side hustle, any cash granny gives you, and put it in the market and just let it compound."

Dull as it may be, O'Leary says sticking to his 15% rule will put you on track for millionaire status by the time you're 65. And you don't even have to earn six figures (or have a billionaire dad) to do it.

"If you make $68,000 a year, the average salary, and you do this your entire life — just 15% of your paycheck — you'll end up a millionaire at retirement at 65."

That's right, you don't need to make six figures to retire with seven in the bank. That's thanks to the magical power of compound interest — here's why substance matters way more than style when you're saving for retirement.

Taking advantage of compounding requires discipline — consistently saving and investing even when markets feel volatile, or the financial news cycle is overwhelming.

But staying consistent is only part of the equation. Reaching the $1 million mark also depends on key factors, such as when you start investing and the returns your portfolio generates over time.

For example, if you start saving 15% of your income at age 25 and earn a 4% annual return, you'd only need to pull in $67,459 a year to hit the $1 million mark by 65.

Start at 40, however, and you'll need to earn more than double — $155,086 per year — to reach the same goal with a 4% return. (And, for the record, saving over $23,000 would put you over the IRS's annual 401(k) contribution limit.) If you can manage to get an 8% return, on the other hand, the required income drops to $83,563.

Historically, the U.S. stock market has delivered strong long-term returns. The benchmark S&P 500 has delivered an average annual return of 10.51% since 1957, though, of course, past performance is no guarantee of future results (2).

articles.title: Michael Burry of ‘The Big Short’ was asked to give advice to Gen Z: ‘Buy half the house you can afford,’ and ‘If it flies or floats, rent it’
articles.summary: “Art in the eye of the beholder is cheap,” wrote Burry.
articles.body:
With rumors of a market bubble flying around, perhaps even more people than normal are turning to trader Michael Burry's takes on the economy. The investor became a household name after predicting and betting on the 2007 to 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, chronicled in the Hollywood blockbuster The Big Short. Nearly two decades later, with question marks piling up over artificial intelligence valuations, Burry's skepticism of market hype remains alive and well. He said last month that he believes the AI bubble "may burst sooner than later." And the caution Burry has exercised in his investment career appears to extend into his personal finance rules—and the advice he would give to others. Burry shared on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained , that he had been asked to give life advice to a Gen Zer, age 26.

Burry had 10 pieces of advice. The first was to "never stop exercising or learning"; the second was to "accept compromise [in order] to begin relationships." He also suggested "manifest[ing] the power of compounding" and advised: "Never gamble."

He also recommended having kids and being a good parent, and that "if it flies or floats, rent it" (put otherwise, if it is a plane or a boat, don't buy it). Burry suggested that one "be thankful for and to all" and "be charitable."

Burry practices what he preaches: Every month his newsletter donates 5% of its revenues to a given charity. For October 2026, Burry announced the charity would be Siloam Health, a nonprofit medical clinic he "knows well" that supports uninsured, working poor, and newly arrived immigrant and refugee populations who do not qualify for government assistance.

"Art in the eye of the beholder is cheap" was another piece of advice shared by Burry. When a reader asked for clarification, Burry confirmed that it meant life and objects don't necessarily need to be expensive—or have any cost attached—in order for them to be enjoyed.

Burry also advised, "Buy half the house you can afford"—good advice for those seeking to avoid being trapped by large mortgage payments into working at jobs they don't like.

And while the advice is aimed at younger people, who may not have yet built up the savings or salary to get on the property ladder, for many Americans—regardless of their age—affording a home, or half of one, is impossible.

The latest housing affordability index from the National Association of Realtors (NAR) shows a reading of 105.4 for September 2026, the most up-to-date figure. A reading of 100 or more signifies that a family earning the median income has more than enough income to qualify for a mortgage loan on a median-priced home, assuming a 20% down payment.

articles.title: Economia circular: Indústrias do interior de SP reaproveitam resíduos | G1
articles.standfirst: Iniciativas incluem reciclagem de garrafas PET, tratamento e reutilização da água e reaproveitamento de resíduos da produção.
articles.summary: A economia circular cresce no interior de SP com a reciclagem de garrafas PET e o reaproveitamento de água e resíduos para reduzir impactos ambientais.
articles.body:
Investir em sustentabilidade deixou de ser apenas uma preocupação ambiental e passou a fazer parte da estratégia de negócios de muitas empresas. Além de reduzir os impactos no meio ambiente, práticas sustentáveis podem diminuir custos, evitar desperdícios, aumentar a eficiência da produção e fortalecer a imagem das indústrias no mercado.

Entre essas iniciativas está a economia circular, modelo que busca prolongar a vida útil dos materiais por meio do reaproveitamento, da reciclagem e da redução de resíduos.

Em São José do Rio Preto (SP), indústrias de diferentes segmentos têm investido nesse modelo para transformar resíduos em matéria-prima e reduzir o consumo de recursos naturais.

Garrafas pets são recicladas em empresa de São José do Rio Preto — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

Milhares de garrafas PET vazias chegam diariamente a uma indústria do setor de bebidas em São José do Rio Preto. O desafio é dar um novo destino a esse material, que poderia ser descartado após o consumo.

A empresa criou uma estrutura voltada à sustentabilidade, que recebe garrafas de diferentes regiões do país e transforma o material reciclado em matéria-prima para novos produtos.

O processo começa com a triagem das embalagens. Em seguida, as garrafas passam por máquinas que separam os materiais. Depois, são encaminhadas para a moagem e submetidas a análises laboratoriais, que verificam a qualidade do material reciclado.

Com o processamento, cerca de 450 a 500 toneladas de material por mês voltam à cadeia produtiva. Segundo o coordenador de produção, Jonas David Gardezan, o plástico reciclado pode ser utilizado por diferentes setores da indústria.

“Essa garrafa reciclada pode voltar para as indústrias de alimentos ou para o setor têxtil, na fabricação de roupas. As tampinhas e os rótulos que são separadas na máquina, a gente revende pra fazer cabides e baldes”, explica.

A preocupação com o destino dos resíduos vai além das garrafas PET. Materiais que não são processados na própria unidade, como vidro, latas e papelão, são encaminhados a empresas parceiras para reciclagem ou reaproveitamento.

A adoção dessas práticas acompanha uma tendência observada em todo o país. Segundo dados da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), seis em cada dez empresas brasileiras já adotam alguma iniciativa de economia circular.

Nas grandes empresas, o percentual chega a 66%. Entre as médias, a adesão é de 54%, enquanto nas pequenas empresas o índice é de 43%. Os números mostram que o reaproveitamento de materiais e o uso mais eficiente dos recursos estão ganhando espaço no setor produtivo, embora ainda existam diferenças entre empresas de portes distintos.

Milhares de garrafas pets são recicladas e utilizadas em outros setores da economia — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

Água tratada é reutilizada na fabricação de portas e janelas

Em outra indústria de São José do Rio Preto, que fabrica portas e janelas, a economia circular também faz parte da rotina de produção.

A água utilizada no processo industrial passa por tratamento para que possa ser reutilizada. Depois de usada, ela é armazenada em tanques, onde recebe tratamento químico para a remoção das impurezas.

Durante o processo, os resíduos sólidos se depositam no fundo dos tanques, enquanto a água tratada permanece na parte superior, pronta para ser reaproveitada conforme os procedimentos da empresa.

A indústria também dá um novo destino às sobras de alumínio geradas na fabricação. O material é encaminhado para a cadeia de reciclagem, assim como o aço descartado durante o processo produtivo.

De acordo com a gerente de qualidade, Bruna Lima, a empresa registrou uma redução significativa nas emissões de gases de efeito estufa.

“De janeiro a junho deste ano, conseguimos deixar de emitir 60 toneladas de CO₂, o gás carbônico. Isso representa até 240 árvores que deixaram de ser desmatadas”, afirma.

Economia circular faz parte da rotina da indústria de portas e janelas em Rio Preto — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

Setores industriais se destacam na economia circular

Levantamento da Confederação Nacional da Indústria aponta que a adoção de práticas de economia circular varia conforme o segmento industrial.

O setor de equipamentos de informática e eletrônicos lidera o ranking, com 86% de adesão. Em seguida aparecem a indústria de produtos de borracha, com 85%, e o setor de celulose e papel, com 78%.

Ao transformar o que seria descartado em novos recursos para a indústria, as empresas reduzem desperdícios e ampliam o potencial de aproveitamento da matéria-prima.

articles.title: How much Apple stock does former CEO Tim Cook actually own?
articles.summary: Tim Cook took over as CEO after founder Steve Jobs’ death in 2011 but stepped down 15 years later. Here’s how many Apple shares the ex-CEO owns.
articles.body:
Tim Cook stepped down as CEO of Apple in September 2026, ending a 15-year reign. During that time, Cook guided the tech giant toward record revenue, and at one point during his leadership, Apple was the first publicly traded U.S. company to attain a trillion-dollar market capitalization — boosted by sales of products including the iPhone and the iPad.

Here's how much Apple stock former CEO Cook owns and how he accumulated his shares.

Tim Cook owns 3.2 million shares in Apple, according to an October 1, 2026 , SEC filing . That's a tiny fraction of the company's 14.59 billion shares outstanding. Still, the value of Cook's shares in Apple was $1.1 billion, based on a mid-October 2026 stock price of $348.22.

Is Tim Cook the largest individual shareholder of Apple?

Tim Cook is among the largest known individual shareholders of Apple whose own stake is less than 5%. Arthur D. Levinson, who has been an Apple board member since 2000, owned 3.7 million shares, according to a May 2026 SEC filing .

There are no individuals whose ownership in Apple is 5% or more, the threshold that would require a person to disclose their stake under SEC rules. Institutional investors are the largest holders of Apple stock.

Apple's largest institutional shareholders

Institutional investors are the largest holders of Apple stock. Altogether, institutions owned 76.6% of the company's total shares as of October 2026, according to Nasdaq . The Vanguard Group owns the most, with a 9.8% stake, followed by BlackRock (8%) and Vanguard Capital Management (6.6%), based on data compiled by Nasdaq and calculated by TheStreet.

How & when did Tim Cook accumulate his Apple stock?

Tim Cook was rewarded handsomely for leading Apple after founder Steve Jobs' death in 2011. Awards of restricted stock units — which later vested into common stock — were based on meeting performance-based financial goals within the company.

As Apple's revenue rose over the years, so did Cook's compensation. Before he stepped down as CEO in September 2026, Apple posted a profit of $112 billion on sales of $416 billion in its fiscal year 2025. That compared to a profit of nearly $42 billion on sales of $156 billion in fiscal 2012, Cook's first year as CEO.

During Cook's 15-year tenure as chief executive, Apple's stock surged around 25-fold, to $347.72 in late October 2026. At the same time, market capitalization surged from around $370 billion to $5 trillion.

articles.title: ‘There’s nothing temporary about a temporary store’: How Spirit Halloween’s CEO took it from 130 stores to 1,550—and swallowed your mall’s Hot Topic
articles.summary: Steven Silverstein built Spirit Halloween into a 1,550-store giant with vacant buildings, returning workers and a show borrowed from Bloomingdale’s.
articles.body:
Every year after Halloween, Spirit Halloween's stores empty out and the signs come down. To shoppers, the chain disappears, until next September or so, when another store pops up somewhere in the neighborhood. But to Steven Silverstein, it never closes.

"There's nothing temporary about a temporary store," Silverstein, CEO of Spencer Spirit Holdings, told Fortune . "We are 24/7, 365 Halloween, and you just don't see it."

Its stores open for eight to 10 weeks a year, but planning for next Halloween starts before this year's doors close. The rest of the year goes to signing leases, making and shipping millions of costumes, and lining up tens of thousands of seasonal workers.

When Silverstein joined parent company Spencer's in 2003, there were only 130 Spirit stores nationwide. Now, there are roughly 1,600 locations a year. Moody's estimated that Spencer's and Spirit together made about $1.9 billion in 2023 , and Spirit's two-months of operations brings in more than Spencer's. This year, the company completed its purchase of Hot Topic, BoxLunch and Her Universe from Sycamore Partners, giving it more than 3,000 stores across North America.

Spirit is the largest Halloween specialty chain in North America, and its biggest rival is gone. Party City, which sold costumes alongside party supplies, filed for bankruptcy for the second time in Dec. 2024 and closed its nearly 700 stores by the end of Feb. 2025. Now, folks can turn to Walmart , Target or Amazon—or go in person to catch a show at Spirit.

"We don't sell anything anybody needs. We only sell things you have to have," he said. "It's based on wants, not needs."

Silverstein came to Spirit from Linens 'n Things in 2003, well before its 2008 bankruptcy. But the lesson he brought with him came from earlier, at Bloomingdale's, where he started in 1985 under CEO Marvin Traub, who Silverstein credits with bringing retail theater to the forefront. In those days, he said, Bloomingdale's was famous for its country promotions.

"We are in an entertainment business," Silverstein said of Traub's lesson. "We need to use our stories to entertain and delight the customer."

The first Spirit store he saw had none of the bells and whistles you expect of today's modern-day equivalent. The fixtures were made from the very boxes that the costumes came in, simple merchandise boxes wrapped in black plastic, and the checkout counter was made of two-by-fours and cement blocks. Local Halloween shops were opening on every corner, and Party City was [at the time] the main destination.

articles.title: Still sending checks in the mail? It's time to stop
articles.summary: Check fraud is rising even as the number of checks in circulation is declining. If you're still sending them in the mail, it may be time to stop.
articles.body:
If you're still sending paper checks in the mail, consumer advocates say, it's time to stop.

Every time you drop a check in the mailbox, fraud experts say, you put your bank account at risk. Check fraud is rising, even as the number of checks in circulation is declining. In 2025, federal data shows , Americans lost more money to check fraud than to debit card or gift card scams.

Consumers are writing fewer checks these days, but the amounts are larger, and thieves know it.

"Criminals know that when they see a check in the mail, it's less likely to be a $10 check and more likely to be a $10,000 check," said Scott Anchin , senior vice president of strategic initiatives and policy at the Independent Community Bankers of America, speaking to USA TODAY in September.

Paper checks used to be everywhere. By 2024, however, they represented just 3% of all payments in the United States, according to the Federal Reserve .

Consumers used to write checks to pay bills, buy groceries and re-up at the gym. Today, people often write checks for larger one-time transactions, such as paying a contractor or a tax bill.

Larger checks mean higher stakes for fraud

Larger checks mean higher stakes for thieves. Check fraud has been around for ages, but modern tech gives fraudsters new and more powerful tools.

"Twenty years ago, 30 years ago, we were talking about solo operators," Anchin said. "Now, you have real organized criminal gangs who engage in check fraud. They steal checks en masse. And then they have an incredible amount of technology they can use to alter the check or to create new checks out of whole cloth."

While electronic payments have grown increasingly sophisticated in recent years, the paper check hasn't really evolved.

"The check is still fundamentally the same," said Joe Bernardo, head of fraud and claims at Wells Fargo, in a September interview. "And fraudsters are always looking for weak points in the process to exploit."

Thieves pull checks from residential mailboxes and fish them out of USPS drop boxes. Larger operations steal entire bags of mail.

Once the criminals have your check, they can "wash" your name off with acetone, bleach or rubbing alcohol, said Adam Rust, director of financial services at the Consumer Federation of America, speaking in September.

The thief can change the amount and the payee and deposit the check themselves. Or, they can leave it blank and sell it on the dark web.

The information on your check alone puts your finances at risk.

"Your account number and routing number appear on the check," Rust said. "It's very personal. It's very sensitive."

articles.title: Warren Buffett Has 1 Piece of Advice for Investors Worried About a Crash, and History Proves It Works
articles.summary: The "Oracle of Omaha" has simple advice for anxious investors.
articles.body:
Investors are afraid. That's the conclusion of CNN's Fear and Greed Index. The index incorporates seven indicators, including market momentum, stock price strength, and market volatility. CNN's index has spent most of the last two months hovering between a level of "fear" and "extreme fear."

Warren Buffett has one piece of advice for investors worried about the stock market and a potential crash. And history proves it works.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images. Image source: Getty Images.

Buffett said in a 2016 interview with CNBC, "The money is made in investments by investing, and by owning good companies for long periods of time." Those 18 words pack a powerful punch.

The first part of Buffett's statement might seem unnecessary. It only makes sense that the way to make money in investments is to actually invest. However, one of the biggest mistakes investors make is staying on the sidelines. Wayne Gretzky echoed Buffett's sentiment with his observation about playing hockey, "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take."

Note that Buffett didn't say to buy the hottest growth stock on the market. He emphasized "owning good companies." What does it take for a company to measure up? Consistent financial performance, a durable economic moat, a strong (and honest) management team, and a reasonable valuation rank at the top of the list.

Importantly, though, Buffett doesn't think most people should try to pick individual stocks. He told CNBC in a 2017 interview, "The trick is not to pick the right company. The trick is to essentially buy all the big companies through the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and to do it consistently."

The legendary investor also stressed holding investments for a long time. How long did he mean? Buffett wrote to Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA) (NYSE:BRKB) shareholders in 1989 that his "favorite holding period is forever." He qualified that statement, though, by saying that it applied only to "outstanding businesses with outstanding managements."

Again, though, buying an S&P 500 index fund, such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT:VOO) or the State Street SPDR Portfolio S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT:SPYM), doesn't require an investor to determine whether a business is outstanding or has an outstanding management team. Companies that succeed (based on retaining a high market cap) remain in the S&P 500 index with a greater weight, while those that don't see their weight decline, and they may even eventually get replaced.

articles.body:
The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have added 12% in 2026 despite a number of economic headwinds. That puts both indexes on pace for their fourth consecutive year of double-digit gains for the first time since the late 1990s.

However, investors recently got bad news about the economy. Inflation accelerated in September, as President Trump's decision to take military action against Iran continued to pressure energy prices. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Higher interest rates threaten the stock market in two ways. They make bonds look more attractive relative to stocks, potentially drawing capital away from equities. They also raise borrowing costs for businesses, creating a direct headwind to corporate profit growth.

President Donald J. Trump sits with hands clasped, surrounded by government officials in the Oval Office. Image source: Official White House Photo.

Accelerating inflation makes further interest rate hikes more likely

Inflation accelerated in September as the Iran war continued to disrupt global oil supplies. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 3.7%, the highest reading since May, topping the consensus estimate of 3.6%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Perhaps more concerning, core CPI increased 2.6% in September, the highest level since June. Core CPI measures underlying inflation by excluding volatile food and energy prices. The acceleration suggests that elevated energy prices are bleeding into other areas of the economy by raising manufacturing and transportation costs.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed on multiple occasions to restore price stability by returning inflation to its 2% target, a level last seen more than five years ago. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point in September, and the latest inflation data makes further rate hikes more likely.

Indeed, CME Group 's FedWatch tool shows the most likely outcome is a second quarter-point rate hike at the December meeting, followed by a third quarter-point rate hike at the March meeting. That would bring the target range on the federal funds rate to 4.25% to 4.5%, a level last seen in August 2025.

From his role in the Trump administration to the growing influence of SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX] and Tesla [NASDAQ: TSLA], Democrats have long been eyeing Elon Musk and his vast business network and, according to Politico, the list of possible investigations into Musk is growing.

The billionaire appears to be getting ahead of the potential probes, vowing retribution against any Democrat who takes action against him.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword," Musk wrote on X , replying to a post featuring Politico's article. "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

According to Politico, Democrats are weighing investigations into Musk's time leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and his government contracts, as well as his alleged role in placing restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield networks in Ukraine, which are used by the Ukrainian military.

DOGE was established within days of Trump's inauguration, and Musk was tasked with heading the department that was meant to reign in alleged government overspending.

Politico is reporting that members of House Oversight and other panels are looking to examine Musk's role in the department, which saw the removal of over 250,000 federal jobs and the dismantling of USAID.

The billionaire originally claimed DOGE would reduce government spending by $2 trillion , but later scaled it back to $1 trillion before saying it would save roughly $150 billion in the 2025 financial year. DOGE's official government website claims it saved $215 billion , though critics have said the number is exaggerated.

Musk admitted in an Oct. 20 interview with "The Builders" podcast that he got " carried away " while working with the Trump administration, agreeing with the host that he appeared to get "too intoxicated" by his proximity to power.

"Yeah, I think that's true," said Musk. "I got carried away, basically."

articles.body:
The job market is rough right now; many would-be entry-level workers are still on the hunt.

A new Twitch show hopes to help answer labor market questions and offer job seekers advice.

So far, they've advised callers on everything from salaries to highlighting unique experience.

When Hans Romine finished his architecture degree in 2025, the 24-year-old began looking for work . After about 50 job applications yielded a single interview appointment, he started feeling despondent.

That's when a friend told him about a new show called 877UNMPLYD.

The show is on Twitch , a streaming platform favored by gamers and fans, but has an unlikely host: Jeremy Zimmer , the former CEO of United Talent Agency, along with digital-savvy producer Rachel Braun. The show offers career advice, discusses labor market news, and fields live call-ins from people looking for work.

When Romine called in, he mentioned he'd spent a few months as a recreation supervisor, building morale at an isolated research station in Antarctica. Zimmer and Braun found that the most interesting part of his whole story, and told him to play it up in applications and interviews.

Romine took their advice, and when he went in for that interview, he highlighted his experiences out on the tundra. After he landed the job, he called back in to let the hosts know.

That's the kind of win Zimmer and Braun hope to replicate. Over their first season, the duo hosted 12 episodes, with one episode filmed live on the streets of New York garnering over 54,000 views.

The show is a small experiment in career guidance at a moment when the entry-level job market is getting harder to navigate — especially in New York City . A new report from Partnership for New York City, a nonprofit business advocacy group, found that the number of entry-level jobs has shrunk disproportionately among professions highly exposed to AI; entry-level postings in design, media, and writing fell by 40.6%.

Nationally, employment in white-collar industries has fallen, even as output has gone up — indicating that AI might be effectively replacing entry-level white-collar work.

That dearth of entry-level opportunities is part of what spawned the show, a partnership between TikTok savant Adam Faze and the economic mobility nonprofit Schultz Family Foundation. Judith Dubin, the head of content at the foundation, said that they'd drilled down on investments in career navigation after recognizing how difficult it is to be graduating from high school or college into the current labor market.

articles.title: How do you help a spouse who’s buried in debt? An expert weighs in
articles.summary: The source of your spouse’s debt problems should inform how you both approach the issue.
articles.body:
EDITOR'S NOTE: This story was originally featured in the Savings Challenge newsletter, which you can sign up for here . The weekly newsletter offers readers savings tips, expert answers to your questions and weekly challenges to help boost savings. If you'd like to have a savings question answered by our experts, please send it to savingschallenge@cnn.com .

If your partner is in a tough spot financially and you want to help cure the problem, you might take a beat to consider the circumstance holistically before doing anything.

In this week's Ask the Expert for CNN's Savings Challenge , Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, offers one reader advice on the best way to approach the issue of his wife's large debts.

The reader wrote: " Hi Doug, my wife has $20k in credit card debt and $100k+ in student loans. She's not the best at managing her money and I want to help her with a plan to manage her debt. How can I help?"

DOUG: First, let me just say that the fact that you want to help her says a lot about you. But let me reframe this just a bit because I think it is going to matter.

You said she's "not the best at managing her money." Before doing anything, I'd encourage you to get curious about why she ran up so much debt. Does she have anxiety around money? Was she never taught how to manage it? Or did she run up credit card debt because her income wasn't enough to cover her basic living costs?

The answer changes everything about how you help her. For instance, if she racked up debt to pay for essential expenses over time, no debt payoff strategy will work until the income side gets addressed too.

But if that's not the issue, here's how I'd suggest you and she approach the debt itself. The credit card debt is the most urgent. Those rates are likely somewhere between 20% and 29%, which is brutal. That gets attacked first, aggressively. For the student loans, you need to know the interest rates before deciding how hard to push. Federal loans may have income-driven repayment options or even forgiveness pathways depending on her profession, so don't just throw money at them before understanding what you're working with.

For a practical starting point, try the avalanche method. That's when you pay minimums on everything, then throw every extra dollar at the highest-rate debt, so it gets paid off first. It's mathematically optimal. Some people, however, prefer the snowball method (smallest balance first) because the psychological wins keep them motivated. Both work. I like avalanche but she should pick the one she'll stick with.

Her name is Judy Shelton. And she has spent years developing a proposal that would give buyers of certain government bonds a powerful choice. You can take repayment in dollars — or collect a predetermined amount of gold.

On Oct. 9, the Treasury announced (2) that Shelton would serve as a counselor to Bessent, advising him on currency policy, with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China.

That puts the architect of a gold-linked borrowing proposal inside the department responsible for financing the federal government.

Shelton outlined the mechanics in a 2012 paper (3) published in the Cato Journal, proposing instruments called "Treasury Trust Bonds."

These bonds would pay no periodic interest, and at maturity, holders could choose between a fixed dollar payment and a specified quantity of gold. For investors worried about the dollar losing ground against the metal, that option could make Washington's debt more attractive.

Shelton argued that buyers who expect gold to be worth considerably more than the promised dollar payment — because they "suspect too many dollars will be printed in the meantime" — would pay a substantial premium for that escape hatch.

articles.title: Gen Z is treating the midterms like a market event. Boomers are treating them like weather
articles.summary: A survey finds 72% of Gen Z investors have changed their portfolios ahead of the midterms, versus 17% of boomers. Here’s what it means.
articles.body:
Gen Z investors are scrambling to protect their portfolios from political uncertainty as the midterms approach, but their anxiety could end up costing them.

A whopping 72% of Gen Z investors said they had already made changes to their retirement savings or investment portfolios in anticipation of the November elections , according to a survey from the Nationwide Retirement Institute. That's far more than the 17% of Baby Boomers who reported doing the same.

But the gap isn't a stampede for the exits. About as many Gen Z investors added money to take advantage of current conditions as moved into safer investments, according to the survey. The first generation to grow up with free trades on their phones is treating the election as a market event.

Boomers' decision to wait it out may be less about hard-won wisdom than about where they are in life. Most boomers are drawing down their savings or close to it, so a portfolio "change" for them usually means selling. They're also more likely to already have an adviser — 43% do, according to Northwestern Mutual — and for shares held in taxable accounts, holding until death lets heirs skip the capital-gains bill entirely.

Across all generations, 40% of investors have made changes ahead of the election on Nov. 3, which will determine which party controls either chamber of Congress.

Mark Hackett, the chief market strategist for Nationwide's Investment Management Group, told Fortune that younger investors aren't necessarily more fearful than older generations. Instead, they are changing the way they interact with financial markets as well as how they react to the massive amounts of financial information and trading tools at their fingertips .

"Younger investors came of age in an environment where investing is highly mobile, social and increasingly real-time, so adjusting a portfolio can feel less like a major decision and more like an ongoing process with almost no friction between a headline, an investing app and a potential portfolio adjustment," Hackett said.

That accessibility can be both good and bad. While younger investors have unprecedented access to financial information, it also means they have more opportunities to make impulsive decisions based on breaking news instead of a company's financials or an analysis of economic conditions.

"The question, therefore, is less about risk tolerance or volatility, and more about whether greater access to information is improving decision-making or simply increasing the temptation to trade," Hackett said. "The latter can be fatal for portfolio longevity."

A $5 price hike in 2024 will cost T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) a "reimbursement" agreement of "$38 million in value" for New York customers, state Attorney General Letitia James' office announced on Oct. 20. And it all stems from T-Mobile's pledge to 4G customers to "never change the price you pay" via their "Price Guarantee Plans" between 2017 and 2019.

The AG's office says that, in 2024, T-Mobile did change their price — upping it by around $5 for each phone line. They added that "T-Mobile hid terms in fine print on its website that supposedly gave it the right to raise customers' rates," violating New York law around "hidden or fine print disclaimers," while impacting more than 250,000 state phone plans.

"New Yorkers deserve clear and honest prices, not misleading offers with hidden fine print," James added in the announcement. "Consumers shouldn't have to pay the price for a misleading sale."

James' office told Moneywise they started investigating T-Mobile's price hikes in 2024 and that the reimbursement doesn't mean the company is cutting a $38 million check. Rather, they said, it's an expression of the value of the offers available for those who qualify.

T-Mobile essentially told Moneywise the same, noting that the $38 million is "not the amount in refunds or payments."

What, then, does the $38 million "in value" mean for the customers who had their prices hiked?

The attorney general's office noted that the $38 million is the maximum value of the benefits impacted customers can choose as a reimbursement.

For example, according to the settlement agreement , those eligible customers who choose to cancel their plans could receive "T-Mobile's payment of their last month's recurring charge and a $25 cash card."

Eligible customers who stick with T-Mobile can choose from "either a free or discounted 5G-equipped wireless phone for each line experiencing less than 5G service," along with T-Mobile's promise "not to increase the monthly recurring charge on the account's current plan until no earlier than May 30, 2029."

articles.title: Americans have never had more of their money in stocks — not even in the dot-com bubble: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Your parents' nest egg was mostly bonds and savings accounts. Yours is mostly stocks.
articles.body:
Your parents' nest egg was mostly bonds and savings accounts. Yours is mostly stocks.

Stocks made up 48.2% of Americans' financial assets in the second quarter, counting everything from brokerage accounts to 401(k)s, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Financial Accounts data. That's the highest share in records going back to 1945. It tops the 38.7% reached at the height of the dot-com mania and the 41% hit after the 2021 meme-stock frenzy.

The cash pile looks small by comparison. Households hold about $74 trillion in stocks against roughly $20 trillion in bank deposits and money market funds — a record $3.65 in stocks for every dollar of cash.

So much for all that money waiting on the sidelines.

There's some fine print. The Fed's household category is a catch-all that also includes nonprofits, and the central bank says its estimates for the group are "largely residual, derived from other sectors' data."

The ownership is lopsided, too. The richest 1% of households own about half of all stocks and stock funds, and the top 10% own 88%, according to the Fed's distributional data . The bottom half owns about 2%.

America isn't all in on stocks. Wealthy America is.

Most of the climb also came from rising prices, not a buying spree. When stocks rally and everything else sits still, stocks take up a bigger slice of the pie on their own.

History suggests a crowded trade tends to deliver less.

When stocks made up less than 20% of household financial assets, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) went on to gain a median of about 11% a year over the next decade, according to Yahoo Finance calculations using price returns since 1951. When the share topped 30%, that fell to about 5%.

The logic is simple. A low share means plenty of money is left to move into stocks, usually at bargain prices. A high share means much of that buying has already happened, and valuations are stretched.

It's a decade-long signal, not a timing tool. Most of the high readings came from the late-1990s bubble and the years before the 2008 financial crisis. Today's level is beyond anything in the record.

What it can do is prompt a portfolio checkup. An investor who set a 60/40 mix of stocks and bonds at the start of 2023 and never rebalanced would now have about 73% in stocks, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

That's a lot more risk than they signed up for.

With this much wealth tied to the market, a sell-off like the one hitting AI stocks can dent consumer spending faster than it used to. Household balance sheets still have room to absorb one.

articles.title: 'It's not something that gets done overnight': SpaceX's telecom ambitions will be hard-won, CEOs and analysts say
articles.summary: SpaceX's challenge to the US telecom industry will be costly and time-intensive, analysts and CEOs say.
articles.body:
Elon Musk wants SpaceX ( SPCX ) to take on America's largest cell service providers, but matching the telecom giants' vast wireless networks could take years and billions of dollars, executives and analysts warned this week.

SpaceX, which already operates the world's largest commercial satellite network with Starlink, is in talks with major telecommunications infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States, Bloomberg reported. The move would advance Musk's ambitions to establish a fourth nationwide wireless carrier alongside the three traditional telecom and mobile service incumbents: Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ).

The announcement sent stock in AT&T and T-Mobile falling by as much as 6% on Friday, while Verizon declined by a thinner 1.5%.

Satellite launches through Starlink and spectrum acquisitions "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call.

But breaking into an industry whose dominant players have spent decades building out infrastructure, acquiring spectrum, and cultivating millions of subscribers will be no easy feat.

"It's not something that gets done overnight," AT&T CEO John Stankey told analysts on his company's earnings call Wednesday, before the latest details of SpaceX's plans emerged. "It takes a lot of years and a huge level of investment to get to the kind of performance levels that customers have become accustomed to in scaled networks."

SpaceX's tower negotiations, which reportedly include cell tower operator Crown Castle ( CCI ), represent one of the clearest indications yet of the scale of SpaceX's ambitions. They also illustrate the substantial financial and technological barriers facing Musk as he attempts to challenge America's entrenched telecommunications giants.

The company's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would put its planned network on a scale comparable to that of the three incumbents. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile each lease space on approximately 60,000 to 80,000 US cell towers combined, according to Goldman Sachs analysts, while the country has roughly 175,000 traditional cell towers nationwide, per data from SNL Kagan.

The cost for such a build-out would be immense, even for a company with the capitalization and balance sheet of SpaceX. The average cellular tenant pays roughly $50,000 per year to lease space on a cell tower, according to Goldman Sachs analysts led by Michael Ng. At that rate, an 80,000-tower network could generate approximately $4 billion in annual rental payments, or between $20 billion and $40 billion over a typical five- to 10-year leasing period.

If you've benefited from rising stocks, it might be worth asking how much of your nest egg depends on the boom continuing.

For years, corporate buybacks and acquisitions have helped take shares off the market. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) alone repurchased 402 million shares for $89.3 billion in fiscal 2025 (2).

An IPO also isn't necessarily the end of the selling. Employees, founders and early backers often face lockup periods that temporarily prevent them from unloading their shares.

Kathie Schwartz recently spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to make sure her and her husband had a plan for aging.

This plan isn't just helpful for her friends who haven't yet planned for their future. It also helps protect Schwartz and her friends against social isolation — something that a quarter of Americans aged 65 and older have to deal with.

The California couple is building a community that isn't just blood-related family

Schwartz said that her planned community of tiny homes would let her stay in touch with friends she's close with.

articles.title: ‘She’s living the dream’: My stepmother said I can buy my childhood home for $850,000. Is she taking advantage of me?
articles.summary: “My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s.”
articles.body:
My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s. By the time he died, it was worth about $850,000, mostly because it's spacious and in a good neighborhood. He left it to my stepmother, whom he married a few years after my mom died. She is now 74. They were together for 18 years. She took care of him through the whole illness, which I don't take lightly.

Dad told me more than once that the house would be mine someday. My stepmother now wants to sell and move somewhere smaller. She's living the dream in Miami. I offered $700,000. That's $200,000 under market, but I thought it was fair, given that she would skip agent fees and it would be a quick, clean sale. I'd have to stretch to do it, but I could manage.

She was really offended, and she told me as much. She said she's paid the property taxes and the repairs for years (she put a new roof on in 2021). She also said she spent a big chunk of her own savings on my father's care and that the house is basically her retirement plan, and that she can't just hand me $200,000 because I'm sentimental.

That's a fair point, and I told her so. What I can't get past is that a few years ago she gave her daughter $200,000 toward a house, and that is how (and why) I came up with the $200,000 haircut on my father's home. I brought that up, and she said things were different then, and pointed out that I have a good job and can buy my own place.

She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died. As my girlfriend at the time said, "Yes, she really went there." That comment really stung. He trusted her with everything, and it feels like his wishes just evaporated. She says she honored him by caring for him and that I'm discounting everything she sacrificed.

I could, of course, walk away and buy somewhere else. I've even looked at a couple of listings. But it wouldn't be the same, and I'd always feel like the house slipped away from our family. I know that my stepsister's place has a sauna in the basement, and I'd bet anything that my stepmother helped pay for that too. Not that I'm keeping score. (OK, I know I am a little.)

Worried you might be weighed down with a parent's debts or expenses after they die? You might not need to worry.

As it turns out, you may have limited obligations to pay your parents' debts if they die (or to take on their expenses if they're still alive). And, if you're a parent, there are steps you can take to prevent your adult children from taking on your debts, if you were to die.

There are three types of parental debt that adult children can avoid paying — even if the debt collectors come calling. Here's what you need to know.

Tampa resident Morgan recently called (1) into The Ramsey Show to ask how she can navigate a "super large amount of debt." While she says she has a full-time job, she just graduated three months ago — and she's saddled with her disabled mother's and late father's expenses.

articles.title: Aston Martin's CEO Is resetting the business
articles.summary: Aston Martin's leadership shakeups and billions in investment have yielded little. Can its new CEO turn things around?
articles.body:
The last five years at Aston Martin have been anything but stable. Not only is the automaker dealing with evolving emissions regulations but also financial instability, product-quality concerns, production delays, and lingering questions about the competitiveness.

There have also been major leadership shakeups. The company is on its third CEO since 2020, with past Mercedes-AMG CEO Tobias Moers (August 2020–May 2022) and former Ferrari CEO Amedeo Felisa (May 2022–September 2024) put out to pasture and previous Bentley Motors CEO Adrian Hallmark taking the reins in September 2024.

Former Lamborghini Americas CEO Andrea Baldi joined the company as Chief Commercial Officer in May.

With Hallmark at the helm, the company is beginning to stabilize across all fronts now that he's wrapped his head around the innerworkings of the company. "[It] took me about three months to basically understand it, and another three months to really understand it," Hallmark told Newsweek .

In his first half-year, Hallmark set up new approaches to the business, established new targets, and started to restructure the company. That's when two rounds of significant layoffs happened.

"A huge amount of equity has gone into this business, nearly $3 billion over six years," the CEO explained. "But everything that was going in was predicated on us hitting 10,000 [unit sales of] cars [annually] relatively quickly. At the same time, the market was coming down."

Hallmark looked at the landscape and knew he had to make the company operate in the black on just 6,000 in annual model sales.

"We've now cut costs. We've changed the operational model of the company, so we can be successful, generate profit in cash at around six, six-and-a-half thousand sales a year, which we can pretty much do every year," he said.

That means that when the company is able to grow its sales, it will be "profitable and safe at that level" Hallmark continued, identifying 2027 as the year of inflection for the company where "the full year, not just part of the year, we're in profit and cash." He expects the second-half of this year to be cash- and profit-generating for the company as well.

Aston Martin is picking up steam heading into 2027. In August it debuted the world's most powerful, front-engined, production supercar, the Valen. Through private viewings to targeted potential customers, the car company already had 400 people view the model privately, before it ever was shown publicly. It's part of a new effort to tap into the 1000 people in Aston Martin's database that have spent more than a million dollars with the brand, Hallmark explained.

articles.title: Meta Unseats Musk as Tech Villain for Lula in Brazil’s Election
articles.summary: A new villain is emerging in the closing stretch of Brazil’s bitterly contested presidential election: Meta Platforms Inc.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A new villain is emerging in the closing stretch of Brazil's bitterly contested presidential election: Meta Platforms Inc.

The social media giant has been ordered by Brazil's electoral court not to interfere with the distribution of political or election-related content after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign accused it of "repeatedly and systematically" failing to deliver his content to users across its platforms. The United Nations has also called out the company, and even US lawmakers are demanding answers.

The spat with Meta is reopening a fight over the power of social media companies that has been brewing in Brazil for years. It's a deja vù of the clash between Brazilian authorities and Elon Musk over his X platform, which escalated into judges ordering the removal of content and accounts accused of spreading disinformation during the 2022 election and culminated in the service being briefly banned in the country two years ago.

At stake is the outcome of the contest to lead Latin America's largest economy. With Lula and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro tied in polls ahead of Sunday's runoff, reaching the right audience could be key in defining the result of the election unfolding in one of Meta's most lucrative markets.

Lula — who has attracted more than 10 million supporters to a WhatsApp channel dubbed "Lula's Army" in recent days — has alleged interruptions to his account, restrictions on Instagram posts and unequal audience engagement. His campaign also said Meta AI, the company's generative artificial intelligence tool, is refusing requests to create images related to Lula while generating campaign material favorable to his opponent.

Spokespeople for Meta in Brazil referred to the company's statement on Oct. 16 pushing back against the interference claims and calling the incidents cited by the Lula campaign as unrelated technical problems rather than evidence of political bias. Meta said that it has taken steps to address those issues and that it treats all candidates equally.

But by then it had already become the target of blame for leftists. Lula supporters have protested alleged election interference in front of Meta's Brazil headquarters in Sao Paulo, and in a letter to Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg, US lawmakers led by Bernie Sanders said they were "deeply concerned about credible reports of Meta platforms restricting or suppressing content."
