articles.summary: Sudan is suffering from a cost-of-living crisis affecting millions across the country.
articles.body:
Azhari Mohamed drives his minibus and eight passengers seven times a day from the Shagar neighbourhood in the Port of Sudan to the city centre and back again.

But despite the long hours – working from 6am to 9pm – fuel shortages in the city have made it difficult for the 60-year-old to make a living.

Azhari’s minibus uses three gallons (11 litres) of petrol a day, costing him about 105,000 Sudanese pounds ($11.30 a day, according to Sudan’s parallel-market exchange rate). With fuel increasingly difficult to obtain, he now spends two days on the road and a third day queuing for fuel.

He can spend more than five hours waiting in line when he needs to fill the tank of his minibus and often finds petrol has run out before his turn comes. When that happens, he goes to the back of the queue at another petrol station hoping to fill up there.

The shortages have led to price rises with a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol now costing 40,000 Sudanese pounds ($4.30) in Gazira State, south of Khartoum, while in Port Sudan it is 35,000 pounds ($3.80) a gallon.

“We can no longer work because of the fuel shortages. The transport fares are no longer enough to cover the cost of running the vehicle and our household expenses,” Azhari told Al Jazeera.

He says the long hours spent queueing for petrol is time he could spend earning money to support his family.

“I spend long hours of the day waiting to refuel, so I have to work extra hours at night to make up for the time I lose during the day,” he said. “My livelihood depends on what I earn each day.”

After subtracting his vehicle’s operating costs, Azhari has just 50,000 Sudanese pounds ($5.40) left a day, barely enough to cover the needs of his family, which includes his wife and daughter who is at university and needs support for her tuition fees and daily expenses.

“We just need fuel to be available so we can work,” he said. “If fuel is available, we will not face this obstacle.”

Due to the crisis, Sudan’s Transport Chambers Union, which regulates public and private transport services, this month raised intercity bus fares by 40% and minibus fares by 30%.

Aziza Ibrahim from the Umm al-Qura neighbourhood of Port Sudan, works as a cleaner to support her four children. Just getting to work by bus has become a huge financial burden for the 38-year-old, who has cut back her work days to three times a week due to the high travel costs.

Before the war, a journey from her home to the main transport station in the city centre cost 700 Sudanese pounds ($0.08) per passenger. Fares have since risen to 2,500 pounds ($0.27) on some routes, while others charge 2,000 pounds ($0.22).

“I go to work three days a week to reduce transport costs. I need 11,000 pounds ($1.18) a day for the round trip between my home and workplace,” she told Al Jazeera.

Transport costs now consume nearly half of Aziza’s monthly salary of 400,000 pounds ($43), while costly treatment for her diabetes is another financial burden.

“Sometimes I have to borrow money just to be able to go to work. I repay it at the beginning of the month when I receive my salary, which is barely enough to cover my family’s needs,” she told Al Jazeera.

According to the United Nations Development Programme, the war has pushed average incomes in Sudan back to levels last seen in the 1990s.

That is partly due to the effects of the civil war on Sudan’s oil sector. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) began on April 15, 2023.

Last year, the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum estimated war-related losses at $20 billion. The World Bank has reported that attacks on the Balila oil field disrupted supplies to the Khartoum refinery, which previously met about 60% of the country’s demand for petrol and liquefied petroleum gas.

War damage has seen a sharp decrease in oil production, leaving Sudan reliant on imports amid the global fuel crisis that has pushed up prices of gas, petrol and diesel, among other commodities.

Economic analyst Sidi Ohaj said that the government requirements for petroleum importers have also contributed to the shortages. They include a stipulation that importers must deposit 200kg of gold in the Central Bank and own fuel storage facilities in order to operate in Sudan. Some importers have been unable to meet those requirements, forcing them out of the market which reduces supply.

“One of the causes of the current crisis is the government’s decision to regulate the operations of petroleum import companies,” Sidi told Al Jazeera. “Some companies did not meet the requirements, which led to their exit from the market. This reduced supply relative to demand.”

The government needs to urgently ease import procedures to increase domestic supplies, he said, with shortages affecting the wider economy.

But as the war between the United States and Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, there is little hope the situation will improve any time soon.

“The continuation of the war [in Sudan], particularly drone attacks that threaten infrastructure across Sudan, is one of the main challenges facing the oil sector,” Sidi told Al Jazeera.

Prices have also risen due to the energy crisis, impacting the purchasing power of citizens and profits of businesses.

Ahmed al-Haj is a local trader in Omdurman market who sells skincare products, such as petroleum jelly, which he packages himself . He said high energy prices are costing almost all areas of his business.

“The raw materials for the products I sell are imported. Higher diesel and petrol prices have increased the cost of transporting a tonne of goods by 30 to 50 percent,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera.

“That increase is then reflected in the price of the products.”

When electricity cuts force him to use a fuel-powered generator for heating or packaging, the additional fuel costs add to his daily bills.

Deliveries within Omdurman, which previously cost 5,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.70) now cost between 10,000 and 12,000 pounds ($1.07 and $1.29). Reaching customers in other states has become impossible due to the high transport costs.

“Transport and distribution workers have also reduced the number of trips they make, leading to goods piling up at traders’ premises,” he added.

articles.title: Will gold hit $5,000 again? What experts expect for 2027
articles.summary: Gold may not hit $5,000 this year, but experts see a possible path back in 2027. Here’s what could drive the next move, and if now is the time to buy.
articles.body:
Gold topped $5,000 per ounce early this year but has since pulled back. While prices started climbing again this summer, the Federal Reserve's September rate hike and the possibility of further increases have created new uncertainty. It's currently trading in the low-$4,000s per ounce.

In short, most experts no longer expect gold to return to $5,000 before the year ends. Still, the longer-term outlook remains optimistic, and another run toward $5,000 is realistic in 2027 if current pressures ease.

Here's where experts see gold prices moving next, and if now could be the right time to buy .

What's the outlook for gold over the next few months?

Gold forecasts have shifted recently as expectations for Federal Reserve policy have changed. In August, Goldman Sachs Research forecast that gold would reach $4,900 per ounce by year-end. But the Federal Reserve's September rate hike and the possibility of further hikes have since created more uncertainty.

Yves Renno, market analyst and head of trading at Wirex , expects gold to trade between $4,000 and $4,400 per ounce through the end of the year. He says central bank buying could support prices, while a strong dollar and another potential rate hike could limit gains.

Analysts are more optimistic about 2027. If interest-rate pressures ease and the dollar weakens, gold could recover, placing a return to $5,000 per ounce within reach. "The long-term fundamentals for gold remain intact," says Nic Puckrin, macro analyst and founder of Coin Bureau .

Higher rates and a strong dollar are weighing on gold

Higher interest rates are a major factor weighing on gold right now. Because gold doesn't pay interest, higher yields can make other investments, like bonds, more attractive to investors. This can reduce demand for gold.

Higher rates can also strengthen the U.S. dollar, creating another headwind for gold. Because gold is globally priced in dollars, a strong dollar means gold is more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

These obstacles explain why earlier forecasts haven't played out yet. Where gold goes from here could depend on whether the Fed continues raising rates. "If traders start to expect more than two or three rate hikes from the Fed in 2027, the dollar has a lot of upside potential, which in turn probably means downside for gold," says Tom Graff, Chief Investment Officer at financial planning firm Facet .

articles.title: Metals Traders Reap Bonanza With Another Year of Record Profits
articles.summary: Metals traders are earning billions of dollars in a second consecutive blowout year for the sector, with several top trading houses notching up record profit...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Metals traders are earning billions of dollars in a second consecutive blowout year for the sector, with several top trading houses notching up record profits.

Trafigura Group, which competes with Glencore Plc for the title of the world's largest metals trader, made a record profit of around $2 billion in metals trading in its financial year that ended in September, according to people familiar with the matter. Glencore, too, has been enjoying some of its best-ever profits, although its overall results have been marred by a $480 million provision related to its exposure to iron ore trader Radiant World.

The vast earnings haul has meant that the champagne was flowing freely at London Metal Exchange Week, the main annual gathering of the global metals industry, which concluded on Friday. Many individual traders said privately they are enjoying the best earnings of their careers, while simultaneously fielding job offers from rival companies, as well as newer entrants looking to grab a slice of the metals boom.

While many had expected fewer opportunities for metals traders after US President Donald Trump did not go ahead with tariffs on refined copper last summer, continued ambiguity over whether tariffs might yet be imposed has extended a bonanza available to traders shipping copper to the US. Meanwhile, metals including copper, gold and silver have soared to record highs, while the market for semi-processed copper concentrate — the bread-and-butter of many physical traders — has been unprecedentedly tight.

Trafigura's metals division has had a record performance in trading, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified as the results aren't public. The trading house is still finalizing its results, which it usually reports in early December, and the audited profit numbers might be subject to adjustments and revaluations of assets like its smelting unit, Nyrstar, some of the people said.

Trafigura and Glencore both declined to comment.

Mercuria Energy Group, the most aggressive of a group of energy traders that have expanded in metals in the past few years, has also had a strong year. Mercuria's annual operating profits are on track to match or exceed last year's level above $300 million, people familiar with the matter said. The company has plowed more than $4 billion into metals deals everywhere from Congolese copper to Indonesian aluminum as it seeks to grow its footprint in the market.

articles.title: We have more clothing options than ever. Why is shopping so hard?
articles.summary: Down a dim, crooked hallway inside the Jay Street Lofts, a hulking brick relic of Brooklyn’s industrial past, Naomi Mishkin is conducting a radical fashion experiment.
articles.body: Down a dim, crooked hallway inside the Jay Street Lofts, a hulking brick relic of Brooklyn’s industrial past, Naomi Mishkin is conducting a radical fashion experiment. She’s making shirts. In New York City. Using cotton and wool. They are not cheap, and they never go on sale. That counts as a rebellious act in the sprawling $1.9 trillion global fashion industry, a business that over the past three decades has mastered the art of cutting production costs to the bone. Mishkin owes some of the success of her label, Naomi Nomi, to a growing backlash against companies – from the luxury tier on down to mall brands and fast fashion – that have tried to pull the synthetic poly-blend wool over our eyes. The middle tier of the market has been hollowed out, with prices inching higher even as brands downgrade quality. Big mall brands aren’t seeing sales drop off a cliff, but customers have become “more interested in buying less, but buying right,” Neil Saunders, managing director of retail at GlobalData, said. “There is a bit of a disconnect between what consumers are looking for and what’s being delivered,” he added. Shoppers may feel constrained by higher inflation, but they aren’t trading down to cheaper brands. “Consumers are looking at value more closely and part of that involves assessing how long garments will last and how much wear consumers will get out of them.” Mishkin, who launched Naomi Nomi in 2018, says her average customer starts with one shirt, then comes back for three more within six months. “I don’t f**k with my quality… That is the reason I’m still kicking. And I want to be a business that’s around for the next 50 years.” Yes, it is going to be pricier Inside Mishkin’s sunlit studio, spools of thread, scissors and power tools hang on a peg board above a worktable. There are three racks of shirts and a mirror by the window, with a curtain that can create a makeshift dressing room. It is not a typical retail experience. There’s no storefront. No sale racks or cash registers or crowds. Try-ons are by appointment. And if you decide to buy a shirt, you won’t get to walk out with it the same day. The shirts are made to order, so no fabric is cut until the money clears. And the money is no joke: Naomi Nomi’s signature white cotton Oxford button-down, sewn in a factory a few miles north in Queens, costs $268 before tax. That is nearly four times what I paid for the white Gap button-down that I wore when I met Mishkin at her studio in September. Browsing a rack of her latest merino wool Oxfords ($338 a piece), I’m not even holding a coffee but I am nonetheless anxious about spilling coffee on them. They remind me, favorably, of the elegant-but-sturdy garments that once filled my grandmother’s closet. That is part of Mishkin’s pitch. While she describes her base as “millennials and their mentors” — folks well into their 30s and beyond — there is a younger cohort finding Naomi Nomi because they’d rather have one good $300 shirt than five $60 shirts. They’re increasingly shopping secondhand, she said. And when they buy new, they’re reaching for brands like hers that exist in a kind of obscure fashion middle ground that some in the industry refer to as “advanced contemporary” — cheaper than luxury but well above mass market prices. “They’re sick and tired of the planned obsolescence of it… I think that’s the biggest selling point in my clothing. I’m telling you, ‘Yes, it is going to be pricier than an Anthropologie shirt. We’re pricier than Banana Republic, but we’re going to last.” What happened to retail? For me, it started with one crooked seam. Two years ago, I ordered a seemingly identical replacement of a simple cotton dress that I practically lived in. When the replacement arrived, the new cotton felt stiff, less breathable, and one side seam veered off at an angle, pulling the fabric awkwardly around my body. I chalked it up to a rare miss from an otherwise reliable brand. But subsequent purchases were similarly disappointing. Sweaters quickly pilled after a few wears. Sizing was all over the place. Everything, it seemed, was too delicate for the washing machine. None of what I was buying could be categorized as fast fashion. But there was no denying something had changed. It wasn’t all in my head. A confluence of forces has upended the economics of retail over the past several decades. Fast fashion’s ascendence alongside social media in this century is certainly one well-documented culprit. But the decline of American textile manufacturing since the 1970s played a role, too, as brands went overseas for cheap labor. When I asked fashion podcaster Avery Trufelman where the trouble began, she pointed to, among other things, LVMH CEO Bernard Arnault, whose aggressive overhaul of European fashion houses in the 1980s pushed designers to churn out double or even triple the number of seasonal collections they produced. The result today is that we expect clothes to be cheap, and we expect to buy a lot of them. But that is a relatively new reality. In 1980, the average American bought 12-14 clothing items a year. By 2018, that figure was 68, Dana Thomas, author of the book “Fashionopolis,” which exposes the labor abuses and environmental tolls of fast fashion, told me. And while the price of just about everything Americans buy has gone up since 1980, clothing is a notable exception. Apparel prices in the United States in 2024 were essentially the same as in 1994, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “We’ve been conditioned to think that clothes should be cheap, but they shouldn’t be cheap,” Thomas said. “Labor costs money… they’re only cheap because nobody along the supply chain is paid what they’re worth.” ‘Capitalism 101’ For a growing cohort of style influencers, we’ve reached a tipping point. Rachael Brownfield, a Tampa-based advertising executive who moonlights as a retail sleuth, documents on TikTok her dismay over the fast-fashion-ification of brands such as Madewell and Anthroplogie that she once loved. Two key themes emerge in Brownfield’s videos: Brownfield captures a frustration that’s palpable across the internet: Clothes have never been more abundant. Yet it’s never been harder to shop for them. Global clothing production doubled between 2000 and 2014, according to McKinsey research, and the number of garments purchased per person in that time grew 60%. Today, the fashion industry produces 100 billion garments and accessories every year. That is only a best guess, though, because companies aren’t required to disclose how much they produce, or how much of it ends up in a landfill, Thomas said. About 60% of new clothes now contain some form of plastic, which can include polyester, acrylic and nylon – all of which are cheaper than cotton or linen, but none of which break down naturally. To be sure, a bit of polyester here and there is not inherently bad, especially in outdoor or athletic gear. But it feeds into a consumption loop: Introducing plastic makes an item cheaper to produce, spurring more demand for low-cost items. Shoppers get excited by new trends and brands move quickly to cater to them. Those clothes then cycle through our closets to the thrift store to the landfill as we move on to the next trend. “This is capitalism 101,” Thomas said. “‘Now that we’ve got everybody hooked on the product, let’s see how we can cut the corners on the product to raise our profits, and maybe no one will notice.” But at some point, consumers do notice, she said. “We’re getting to the endgame… There’s only so much you can cut until it really starts showing.” That’s one of the main reasons a Naomi Nomi shirt costs what it costs: Mishkin’s not using cheaper poly blends or shipping her designs overseas to be sewn in bulk. “My seamstresses live in the same city as my customers,” she said. “If a customer is going from a $3 coffee to a $5 coffee, my seamstresses are going from a $3 coffee to a $5 coffee.”

articles.title: Instacart reportedly discussed selling itself with DoorDash and Uber
articles.summary: Instacart might sell itself to a larger competitor.
articles.body:
Instacart might sell itself to a larger competitor, according to multiple news reports

The Information reported Friday that the grocery delivery company has hired an investment bank to help it evaluate its options, and that it's held acquisition talks with DoorDash. And Bloomberg reported that the company has also talked to Uber — although Uber reportedly walked away from those discussions.

Instacart currently has a market cap of more than $13 billion, and its stock price is up 25% for the year to date. The company could see this as a good time to sell at a desirable price, before the grocery delivery market gets more competitive — but Bloomberg noted that these are early discussions that might not result in a sale.

An Instacart spokesperson declined to comment. The reports of a potential sale caused the company's share price to spike more than 9.2% on Friday, while Uber and DoorDash stock declined.

articles.title: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.summary: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.
articles.body: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices. Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years. Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year. “I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’” Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines. U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period. This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars — including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers — for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago. Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa — which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate -- and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February. But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales. Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year. “People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.” The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales. “We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

articles.title: AI bear slams Nvidia's GPU pitch: 'There's not scarcity other than that which is created by Jensen Huang'
articles.summary: Ed Zitron, CEO of public relations firm EZPR and well-known critic of the AI spending boom, says Nvidia is creating the scarcity it sells against.
articles.body:
Ed Zitron, CEO of public relations firm EZPR and well-known critic of the AI spending boom, says Nvidia ( NVDA ) is creating the scarcity it sells against.

Zitron pointed to how concentrated Nvidia's customer base is, saying that five companies accounted for about 70% of Nvidia's accounts receivable in the first half of the year, a risk factor that "Big Short" investor Steve Eisman also recently noted.

"Jensen Huang is channel stuffing. It's obvious," Zitron said on Yahoo Finance's The 8:30 on Friday (video above). "He's forcing GPUs down the channel saying, you have to buy these now, or they won't be available in a few months. I think that's morally reprehensible."

"It's driving up the price of every imaginable consumer electronics. It's making everyone's life worse so that Jensen Huang's life can be better and so that whoever owns Nvidia stock can feel slightly better."

Asked whether Huang's pitch is simply a demand signal, given years-long lead times in semiconductors, Zitron said, "How is there scarcity of a product that they have too many of? There's not scarcity other than that which is created by Jensen Huang."

Zitron also questioned what the data center build-out delivers. "What does more data centers actually get us?" he asked, citing a Bloomberg report that Microsoft ( MSFT ) has about 2 gigawatts of AI compute online out of 12 gigawatts reported, while noting that Amazon ( AMZN ) recently canceled a data center in Loudoun County, Va.

He has argued that OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) have become "load-bearing" for Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG ), Amazon, CoreWeave ( CRWV ), and Nebius ( NBIS ). Asked what should happen if they falter, he didn't hesitate: "Let them die."

The hosts pushed back, noting that a record share of Americans own stocks and that some, including Bloomberg's Eric Balchunas, have argued that could pressure the government to step in during a crash. Zitron said a rescue wouldn't hold the market up anyway. "You can bail them out all you want, but unless everyone's buying more and more GPUs at more and more high prices, it's going to crash either way," he said. "The GPU sales are what matter. That's what's keeping the market alive."

articles.title: IDFC First Bank Q2 profit nearly triples to Rs 1,045 crore; loan assets rise 30%
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: IDFC First Bank reported a 196.5 per cent year-on-year jump in profit after tax to Rs 1,045 crore in the September quarter of FY27, supported
articles.body: NEW DELHI: IDFC First Bank reported a 196.5 per cent year-on-year jump in profit after tax to Rs 1,045 crore in the September quarter of FY27, supported by strong growth in core operating profit and an improvement in asset quality.Core operating profit, excluding trading gains, rose 38.5 per cent to Rs 2,527 crore. Net interest income (NII) increased 21 per cent to Rs 6,184 crore, while fee and other income grew 24.5 per cent to Rs 2,285 crore.Total loan assets, including credit substitutes and loans backed by foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR(B)) deposits, rose 30.1 per cent year-on-year to Rs 3,46,913 crore as of September 30, 2026. Excluding FCNR(B)-backed loans, growth stood at 22.2 per cent on a gross basis, including inter-bank participation certificates (IBPC).Total deposits increased 25.9 per cent year-on-year to Rs 3,48,583 crore. The bank mobilised Rs 34,390 crore in FCNR(B) deposits during the quarter, taking advantage of its digital capabilities despite having no branch, subsidiary or representative office outside India.The bank said the FCNR(B) deposits, largely carrying tenures of three to five years, would provide structural liquidity in the coming years. Their fully loaded cost, including priority sector lending benefits, is approximately 1 per cent lower than the cost of raising domestic fixed deposits.The bank's average current account and savings account (CASA) ratio stood at 48.4 per cent during the quarter, compared with 50.1 per cent in the preceding quarter. Management attributed the decline primarily to the large mobilisation of FCNR(B) deposits.Asset quality improved, with gross non-performing assets (GNPA) declining to 1.32 per cent from 1.86 per cent a year earlier. Net NPA stood at 0.40 per cent, against 0.53 per cent in the year-ago period. Credit cost, as a percentage of average assets, declined to 1.01 per cent in Q2 FY27.The bank's return on assets (RoA) stood at 0.93 per cent for the quarter, while core RoA improved to 0.92 per cent from 0.88 per cent in the June quarter, excluding interest received on an income tax refund in Q1 FY27.Management said operating expenses had grown more slowly than income by over 500 basis points year-on-year for two consecutive quarters. The core cost-to-income ratio improved to 70.16 per cent in Q2 FY27 from 70.73 per cent in the preceding quarter.The bank also said the benefits of FCNR(B) deposit mobilisation, cost savings, product changes and expected repo rate increases could broadly offset the anticipated impact of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's consultation paper on insurance commissions on profitability in FY28.You use AI every day.
